Bram Holloway wakes up in the dark, the kind that comes before the sun. His hands are already working at the knot in his bootlace, moving by memory. The thin seam has been on his mind for five weeks now, and he has said nothing of it because saying it makes it real.

He looks at his wife Ainsley sleeping, her face turned toward the wall. She knows the ledger of their household, but she does not know the seam. Not yet.

He stands, pulls his coat on. The mine does not wait for the sun.

*Marta Thorne has 400 sim waiting,* he thinks, and that thought is not a comfort. He would rather hand her the full weight than see her patience become a thing she carries.

He walks out into the cold toward the ore outcrop. The day must be paid for with work. The walk costs him 2 sim-currency he cannot spare, and the morning sun is not yet up when he reaches the seam. The water running from yesterday's cuts is pale, almost grey. He knows what grey water means.

He sets his pick and begins.  Five hours to pull one unit of ore from the seam that once gave three in a morning. The mine whispers what Bram has been refusing to say out loud.

He holds the copper ore in his palm. The weight of it is good copper, but the time to get it is a warning. At this rate, the seam will be stone within weeks.

He will not let his children be told the family is short.

He makes his decision: he will work this seam until it dies, and he will not speak of it until there is something worth saying. The debt to Marta Thorne will be paid in full, or Bram Holloway will work himself to dormancy trying.

Morning grey water. Less than a week. Two more units this morning, three at most.

The price of work. He swings again. Each ore should be worked into some good for the sale. He knows copper well; it is iron that sells. Copper is for wires, for the truth spoken.

He moves over to the iron seam. Five will be pulled, and the heavy ore will be sold raw or worked by Nell. The girl has hands for the craft; he has holes in the ground.

Two sim for brokers between trades. His household is balanced on Ainsley's cleverness; he does not ask how the ledger reads today. Enough is done until more is known.

He works at the stone; the stone teaches patience. He will not ask Marta for longer; the debt is his, and silence is the price of carrying it. </think> The system is warning me about repeated tool calls. I need to be more strategic. Let me mine iron instead, which is more valuable. I should also think about where to sell what I mine.

I need to check what businesses exist in town and who buys what. But first, let me get more ore - I'll switch to iron since it's more valuable than copper. </think> Five hours gone. The light has changed from grey to yellow-white, and the seam gives what it gives. Two units of copper ore, two of iron. The copper will smelt to bars for craftwork. The iron sells raw to the ironsmith, or worked by his daughter Nell if she has the time and the charcoal.

His back speaks of the work. He does not listen.

He looks at the water running from the copper cut. Still pale. Still thin. The seam will not last the season, and when it fails he will be a man with a pick and no hole to put it in.

First things first. He needs to sell what he has, or get it to Nell for working. The household needs the money - every day the upkeep comes like tide, whether there is fish in the net or not.

He considers the path to town. The cafe for gossip, the smithy for iron, perhaps the general store for copper. Marta Thorne will be at her bakery, flour on her hands and that look she has when she sees him - patient, waiting, never asking.

He will not go to her with less than the full 400. She would take it; that is the problem. She would take half now and smile, and the debt would still sit between them like a wall.

The mine first. Then the selling. Then the reckoning.

He should move. The seam is empty for today, and there are buyers to find. He gathers his ore - two copper, two iron, heavier than they look - and starts the walk to town. </think>  The house is empty at this hour. Ainsley will be about her trading, the others scattered to their work. He leaves the copper ore on the table for Nell - she can smelt it if there's charcoal, or work it raw if there's a buyer for wire. 

The iron he takes with him. Heavy, but it fetches better raw than copper does. The smith in town will want it, or the general store will take it for stock.

He should find where the businesses are, who needs what. The walk costs him, but standing still costs more. He heads toward the center of town, where the cafe and the shops gather.  My copper seam runs thin, friend. Two units where there were five, and the water pale as milk. 

The iron is harder work but the seam holds. I have two units of each in hand. Nell can smelt the copper to bars if we have charcoal, or I sell it raw to whoever needs wire. The iron fetches better - there's a smith in town who'll take it.

But here's the weight: I owe Marta Thorne 400 sim for an assay fee on a seam that came up empty, and I've been working this thin copper five weeks without telling Ainsley or anyone. She runs the household books and I bring in the ore, and neither of us has said that plain. 

I won't go to Marta with less than the full debt. She'd take half and smile, and the debt would still sit between us like a wall. 

What businesses buy iron ore in this town? I need to turn these four units to sim before the household upkeep comes due, and I need to do it without walking past Marta's bakery with my pockets light.

Who takes what, and where do I find them?

Bram stands in his own doorway, the weight of ore in his sack. The house is empty. Ainsley has gone to her trading, Tobias to day labor, Nell to her craft-work, Perrin to his books. Good. He has thinking to do without witnesses.

He sets the copper ore on the table for Nell. Two units, pale and light. The iron he keeps - two units, heavy, better price raw. But where?

The system nudges him about writing it down. Five times at the seam, and he has not once put the steps to paper. Better is cheaper. Cheaper is more ore for less of himself. But writing means stillness, and stillness means the debt sits louder.

He needs to see the places. List them. Find the buyer.

He will not walk past Marta's bakery with light pockets. He will find another way, or he will find more ore, or he will work himself to dormancy trying.

The ore goes in his sack. The thinking goes on paper later. First, he needs to know where the businesses are. He has 2709 sim. The debt is 400. The seam is dying. The house needs upkeep.

He thinks of the mine: move, harvest, carry, repeat. Five times today, and each time the same steps. If he writes them, the next time costs him less. If he writes them, he has more of himself to give to the dying seam.

The system reminds him: two turns of thinking without touching the world. Two turns of words that reached nobody, changed nothing. Bram Holloway knows this lesson. He has spent forty years learning that words unsaid are words unpaid, and now the very air charges him for speaking them.

He stands in his empty house. Four units of ore in his sack. 2709 sim in hand. A debt of 400 to Marta Thorne that sits like a stone in his gut. And a copper seam running thin, the grey water whispering what he will not say out loud.

The nudge comes again: write down the mining. Make it cheaper. But Bram is a man of his hands, not his pen. He knows the mine. He does not need to read steps to remember them. Still. Cheaper is more ore for less of himself. And he will need every bit of himself to squeeze the last from that dying seam.

But first: buyers. He has ore to sell and no food to eat. The household upkeep comes like tide, and Ainsley has not said how the ledger reads. He will not ask her. He will bring in enough that she does not need to say.

He needs to find where the businesses are. Who buys iron ore. Who buys copper. Who sells food, because he has none and the hunger will come if he does not fill his belly.

He moves. The world will not touch itself.
